title: Quickselect & divide and conquer
summary: Split the problem, solve the parts, combine. Merge sort splits in half and merges; quickselect partitions around a pivot and recurses into only the side that holds the answer.
idea: One partition puts the pivot in its final sorted place. If that is index k − 1 you are done; otherwise throw away the side that cannot hold it.

signals.see: You need the k-th smallest or largest value, or the median, once, and the order of the rest does not matter.
signals.think: Quickselect: partition, then recurse into one side only. Average O(n) time, O(1) extra space.

signals.see: You must count pairs that are out of order, or merge answers from two halves.
signals.think: Merge sort: solve each half, then count or combine while merging the two sorted halves.

signals.see: Values must be grouped into three bands, such as below, equal to and above a pivot.
signals.think: A three-way partition (the Dutch flag) sorts them in one pass with three pointers.

phrasings: From a million bids, find the 100th highest without sorting them all.
How many pairs of exam scores are listed with the higher one first?
Sort a row of red, white and blue tokens in one pass, in place.

picture.title: Keep only the side with the answer
picture.alt: On the left, the whole array is sorted to read one position, costing O(n log n). On the right, one partition places a pivot in its final position; the search continues only in the side that contains index k − 1, costing O(n) on average.
picture.caption: Quicksort recurses into both sides; quickselect into one.

code.py:
def kth_smallest(nums, k):
    a, lo, hi = list(nums), 0, len(nums) - 1  #@init
    while True:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2; a[mid], a[hi] = a[hi], a[mid]  #@pivot
        pivot, store = a[hi], lo
        for j in range(lo, hi):
            if a[j] < pivot:  #@scan
                a[store], a[j] = a[j], a[store]; store += 1  #@swap
        a[store], a[hi] = a[hi], a[store]  #@place
        if store == k - 1: return a[store]  #@found
        if store < k - 1: lo = store + 1  #@right
        else: hi = store - 1  #@left

visualiser.inputHelp: Numbers: up to 12 whole numbers between -99 and 99. k: from 1 (the smallest) up to how many numbers you entered. The pivot is always the middle of the window, so every run is the same.

oneLiner: p = partition(lo, hi); if p == k − 1 return a[p]; else keep only the side holding k − 1

exercise.prompt: nums holds only 0, 1 and 2. Sort it in place in one pass and return it. Use a three-way partition: low marks the end of the 0s, high the start of the 2s, and i scans between them. The starter moves i forward after swapping in a value from high, so that value is never checked.
hints: Keep three regions: 0s before low, 2s after high, and unchecked values from i to high.
A value swapped in from high has not been checked yet, so do not move i after that swap.

complexity.why: Each partition scans the current window, and a good pivot halves it: n + n/2 + n/4 + … ≈ 2n. A bad pivot every time gives O(n²). A random pivot makes that unlikely; here the middle pivot keeps runs repeatable.

mistakes: Recursing into both sides, which turns quickselect back into quicksort at O(n log n).
Mixing 0-based and 1-based k, so the answer is one place off.
Always picking the first or last element as pivot, which is O(n²) on sorted input.
In a three-way partition, moving i forward after swapping with high, which skips an unchecked value.

quiz.question: After one partition, the pivot lands at index 4 and you need index 2. What next?
choices: Partition the left side, indexes up to 3
quiz.explain: Everything left of the pivot is smaller, so index 2 is in the left part. The right part can be thrown away.

quiz.question: What is quickselect's average running time?
quiz.explain: Each round scans a window about half the size of the last, so the total is about 2n.

quiz.question: Merge sort counts out-of-order pairs while merging. When the right half's value is taken first, how many pairs does it add?
choices: The number of values left in the left half
The number of values already merged
quiz.explain: Every value still waiting in the left half is bigger and comes earlier, so each forms a pair with it.

interviewTip: Say why you pick the pivot you do. Interviewers like hearing that a random pivot gives expected O(n), and that a fixed middle pivot keeps a demo or test repeatable.
